pr_title: Allow running the Docker image with a non-default group
pr_body:
Closes #60864. Tweak the JDK directories' permissions in the ES Docker image so that ES can run under a different user and group.

These changes assume that the image is being run with bind-mounted config, data and logs directories, and reads and writes to these locations will still fail when both the UID and GID are not the default. Everything should be OK when running with the default GID of zero, however.

**Elasticsearch version** (`bin/elasticsearch --version`):
```
# docker image ls elasticsearch:7.8.1
REPOSITORY          TAG                 IMAGE ID            CREATED             SIZE
elasticsearch       7.8.1               a529963ec236        2 weeks ago         811MB
```

**Plugins installed**: []

**JVM version** (`java -version`):
Bundled JDK

**OS version** (`uname -a` if on a Unix-like system):
`Linux 3.10.0-1127.13.1.el7.x86_64 #1 SMP Fri Jun 12 14:34:17 EDT 2020 x86_64 x86_64 x86_64 GNU/Linux`

**Description of the problem including expected versus actual behavior**:
Previous versions of the docker image (7.5.1) were compatible with admin defined UIDs. This no longer works in image version 7.8.1 due to permissions being made more restrictive within the container. The container will die on startup due to being unable to execute the bundled JDK with the following message:

`could not find java in bundled jdk at /usr/share/elasticsearch/jdk/bin/java`

This is due to the permissions of /usr/share/elasticsearch/jdk/, which do not allow traversal by users other than the default uid 1000 user. I am reporting this as a bug because 1) this used to work before, 2) it breaks existing production environments that attempt to upgrade to newer versions of the image, and 3) the change imposes a mandatory uid number on the host operating system for any programs that need to interact with volumes mounted to the container. (in particular the config and data directories)

Note that the permission problems may extend past ownership of /usr/share/elasticsearch/jdk/. These were not immediately noticed as the inability to execute the bundled JDK masks any other problems.

You can actually run the ES image with a different UID, but if you change the GID then you'll run into the problem described here.

I think the root cause of the issue is probably the upgrade in 7.7.0 from OpenJDK 13 to 14. We don't fiddle with the JDK permissions in the Dockerfile, the image just inherits the perms from the ES distribution.

I can tweak the Dockerfile to make sure that the `./jdk` directory has acceptable permissions, but we might want to think about how far we want to support running ES with a different UID / GID. For example, when running:

    docker run -it --rm -u 1001:1001 -e 'discovery.type=single-node' elasticsearch:test 

If I fix the group perms of the directories under `./jdk`, ES still won't start because it can't read `./config/elasticseach.yml`. If I allow that, then it fails because it can't write to `./logs/gc.log`. You can see where this is going. An obvious workaround is to bind-mount your own `config` and `logs` directories.

@blightbow given the above, can you share a few more details about how you're running Elasticsearch? Would just fixing the `./jdk` permissions be sufficient?

I hesitate to mention this, but another option would be to allow the UID and GID to be reconfigured at runtime, [per this example](https://docs.openshift.com/container-platform/3.6/creating_images/guidelines.html#use-uid) (note that the latest version of that document has removed that example). The downside is that we'd have to default to running the container as `root` again, which we wanted to get away from.

> You can actually run the ES image with a different UID, but if you change the GID then you'll run into the problem described here.

Whoops! You're right. I had overlooked the fact that the container starts as root and drops the user privilege, but keeps the gid of 0.

> An obvious workaround is to bind-mount your own `config` and `logs` directories.
>
> @blightbow given the above, can you share a few more details about how you're running Elasticsearch? Would just fixing the `./jdk` permissions be sufficient?

We were already mounting `config` and `logs` in our environment, so I agree that correcting the permissions on `./jdk` would be the way to go. There shouldn't be need for anything fancier than this unless there are other files the JDK needs to read from that have changed in the interim. (unlikely if the JDK upgrade resulted in the permission changes)

Here is a full list of our mounts. I'm pretty sure only `./jdk` needs fixing, the rest should be addressed by mounts.

```
# docker container inspect client | jq .[0].Mounts
[
  {
    "Type": "bind",
    "Source": "/etc/elasticsearch",
    "Destination": "/usr/share/elasticsearch/config",
    "Mode": "rw",
    "RW": true,
    "Propagation": "rprivate"
  },
  {
    "Type": "bind",
    "Source": "/var/log/elasticsearch/client",
    "Destination": "/usr/share/elasticsearch/logs",
    "Mode": "rw",
    "RW": true,
    "Propagation": "rprivate"
  },
  {
    "Type": "bind",
    "Source": "/data/elasticsearch/client",
    "Destination": "/data/elasticsearch",
    "Mode": "rw",
    "RW": true,
    "Propagation": "rprivate"
  }
]
```

review_comments: Should we enforce this in running the image itself?

According to the [docker run documentation](https://docs.docker.com/engine/reference/run/#user), you have to specify the user or UID, so I don't believe that's necessary.

Arguably the API for this test code is weak in that it allows you to pass a `null` uid and a non-null `gid`, but I felt it was overkill to introduce something more robust here.
